parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular present of some -a (first conjugation) verbs. E.g. lucrezi from luc…
parole.testo: Form of the infix -ez-; probably from a Vulgar Latin *-idiās or *-izās, conjugated forms of *-idiō, *-izō, ultimately from Ancient Greek -ίζειν (-ízein), used in Romanian conjugated forms of verbs. See -ez.
From Proto-Romanian, from a late Vulgar Latin *ae(t), from Latin habet.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad vix, from ad + vix. The original form was abi, a variant found in some dialects; the final -a was added by analogy with adverbs like aci(a), aiure(a), acole(a). This suffixation coincided with diphthongisation, turning the stressed -i into a glide. In Banat, however,
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *aboricāre, derivative of Latin orior. Compare urca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, a compound of Latin eccum and ille. Compare Aromanian atsel, Italian quello, Spanish aquel and Catalan aquell.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum + iste. Compare Italian questo, Old French cest, Catalan aquest, and Romansh quest.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) (h)īc, from Latin eccum + hīc. Compare Italian qui, French ici, Spanish aquí, Catalan ací.

Maybe from Vulgar Latin *accēnāre (“to wait until the evening”), originally meaning "to wait until the time of dinner". For the rhotacism of the intervocalic nasal, compare fereastră from Latin fenestra; however, this is uncommon in Romanian, especially without cause of dissimilation. Cf. also the r

parole.significato: hither, here, this way, in my direction
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (ec)cu(m) *hocce, from Latin hoc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) illā(c), from Latin eccum + illāc. Compare Portuguese and Galician acolá, Spanish acullá, Italian colà.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum illōc, from a compound of Latin eccum + illōc. Compare Aromanian aclo, cf. also Portuguese acolá, Ladin chiló.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accoperīre, *accooperīre, from Latin ac- + cooperīre (“cover completely”). By surface analysis, a- + coperi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo. Informal variant of acum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo. Compare Sardinian como.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum modo, from Latin eccum + modo. Variant of acum.

parole.significato: of good quality, beautiful, well-made, fit.
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from acătărea (“good; likely”), originally “any, whichever”, influenced by tare (“strong”), from Vulgar Latin *eccum talis.

parole.significato: to sniff, scent, sense or trace through smell (an animal, person, etc.)
parole.testo: Unknown. Cognate with Aromanian ulmic, ulmicari. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *adosmicāre, from *adosmāre, from Ancient Greek ὀσμάω (osmáō), which would make sense semantically but is difficult to connect phonetically. Compare Italian ormare, Spanish husmear, husmar probably coming from a Latin
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adastāre, from ad- + Latin astāre (“stand at, on, by”), from stō. Compare Aromanian adastu, adãstari.

parole.significato: to smoke (to preserve or prepare food by treating with smoke, as in smoked ham)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affūmāre, ultimately from Latin fūmus (“smoke”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + fum + -a. Compare Aromanian afum. Reinforcement by Italian affumare is possible.

parole.significato: to plunge, immerse, immerge, dip, sink
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affundāre, derived from Latin fundus (“bottom”). By surface analysis, a- + fund + -a. Compare Aromanian afundari.

parole.significato: to loosen, soften, or make a granular material less compact or dense, as with hay
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *affēnāre, from Latin fēnum. Compare French faner, from Vulgar Latin *fenāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *agurāre, from Latin augurāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin agustus < Latin augustus. Mostly replaced by the reborrowing august. Cognate with Sicilian agustu.
From a- + Vulgar Latin *accaptiāre, from a- + *captiāre, from Latin captus. Compare Aromanian acats.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *eas, from Latin habēbās.

From Vulgar Latin *ad hīcce (“to here”), from Latin hīc (“here”), from heic, from earlier forms of hic (“this”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi-ḱe (“this, here”). Compare Italian ci, Sicilian ci, Spanish aquí, Portuguese aqui, Aromanian atsia.
Definite form of albă, from Latin alba, feminine of albus. For the sense of "dawn" or "sunrise", see Vulgar Latin *alba, whence also Spanish and Italian alba, French aube, Portuguese alva.

From a Vulgar Latin root *albaster, albastrum, derived from Latin albus (“white”). Probably originally referred to the whiteness in a lightly clouded sky. See also the formations in Italian biancastro (“whitish”), nerastro (“blackish”), French blanchâtre (“whitish”), noirâtre (“blackish”) (with the
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *albīre, from Latin albēscere. By surface analysis, alb (“white”) + -i.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alvīna (“beehive”) (compare Aromanian alghinã (“bee”), Megleno-Romanian ălbină, Istro-Romanian albire (“bee”), Venetan albina (“hive”), derived from classical Latin alvus or alveus.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *allargāre, from Latin largus (“abundant, plentiful”). Other theories derive it ultimately from a derivation or alteration of Latin legāre or alegāre. Compare Aromanian alag, alãgari; compare also Albanian largoj (“to leave”), Italian allargare (“to widen”).
From a Vulgar Latin root *allenāre, possibly from Latin lenis (“smooth, gentle”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *altru, from Latin alter, alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

From a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from Latin longē. Other theories suggest it deriving straight from Latin ēlongāre. Compare Italian allungare, Catalan allunyar (“move away, remove, distance onself”), French éloigner, allonger, Galician alongar (“move away”), Spanish alongar and Portuguese alonga
From a Vulgar Latin root *abellona, from Latin abellāna, from a city in Italy known as Abella or Avella. Compare Aromanian alunã, Occitan aulana, Portuguese avelã, Spanish avellana.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad lātera, variant of ad latus (“along”) (compare Italian allato, Dalmatian a lič), from Latin ad (“to, at”) + latus (“side”); compare Old French lez (“along”), Spanish al lado (“next to”).

parole.significato: am (modal auxiliary, first-person plural form of avea, used with infinitives to form conditional tenses)
parole.testo: Presumably from a Vulgar Latin *eamus, from Latin habēbāmus.

From a Vulgar Latin root *ammināciāre, *admināciāre, < *mināciō (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”), from the neuter plural of mināx (“threatening”), from minārī (“threaten”). Compare Catalan amenaçar, French menacer, Italian minacciare, Occitan amenaçar, Portuguese ameaçar, Sicilian amminazzari,

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ammixticāre, from ad- + *mixticāre, from Latin mixtus, past participle of miscere (“mix”). Compare Aromanian ameastic, amisticari, Italian mesticare, Dalmatian mescur; also Italian mestare, Asturian amestar, Romansh maschadar, Friulian mesedâ, from a related root.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”). Compare Aromanian amurtsãri.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad modo (compare Dalmatian jamo (“now”), Aromanian amo, acmo). Informal counterpart to acum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amendoi, from ambī duī, from Latin ambō (“both”) + duī, from duo (“two”). Compare Aromanian amindoilji, andoilji. Cf. also Old Italian amendue, Engadine amenduos, Old French andui, Occitan amdui.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ammagīre from *magīre, *magāre, from Ancient Greek μαγεύω (mageúō, “cast a spell; bewitch”), from μάγος (mágos, “magical”); cf. also Latin magus. May be related to Catalan amagar (“hide”) and Spanish amagar (“threaten”), Portuguese esmagar, Sicilian ammagari, although th
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *amarīre, from Latin amarēscere, from amarus (“bitter”).
From amar + -ăcios, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *amāritiōsus, from amāritiēs (cf. amăreață).

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *annināre (“to rock”), from *ninna (“cradle”), from an infantile sound. Compare Italian ninnare (“lull or rock to sleep”), Romansh niner (“to rock”), Occitan nina, Albanian ninuljë. This verb refers to hanging something in an unfixed way, allowing it to rock or dang
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad prope, composed of ad (“to, at”) + prope (“near”). Compare Aromanian aproapea.
Possibly from metathesis of a Vulgar Latin aucupāre, from Latin aucupārī. Other theories suggest Latin occupāre, with meaning influenced by or confused with the former. Compare Aromanian apuc.
From a Vulgar Latin root *appēsāre < *appēnsāre, from Latin pēnsō, pēnsāre (cf. Latin appēndō, appēndere from pēndō, pēndere). Compare Old French apeser, Occitan apesar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *aquatōsus, from Latin aquatus (“diluted, watered down, watery”), from aquor (“get water”), from aqua (“water”). Compare Friulian agadôs.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen n, derived from Latin aer-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ārdĕre, from Latin ārdēre.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *alīnus, from *alnīnus, from Latin alnus + -īnus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élsnos. Compare Aromanian anin, arinu, Megleno-Romanian rin.

parole.significato: Maltese cross (a plant species, (Silene chalcedonica, syn. Lychnis chalcedonica)
parole.testo: From urșinic (“silk”), from an antecedent shared with notable variant urușnic, probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *holoserinicus (“silken”), based on Latin holosēricus. Less likely, a substrate word.

Probably from Vulgar Latin root *excotīre, from Classical Latin cōs, cōtis (“whetstone”). Compare cute and cuțit (“knife”). Cognate with Megleno-Romanian ascut, scuțǫt. Cf. also the semantic evolution of Catalan esmolar (“sharpen”), from mola (“grindstone”). Was also possibly influenced by a Vulgar
From a Vulgar Latin root *astruicāre, from Latin astruere (“build on, heap”).

parole.significato: to stop, close a cover, obstruct, seal, cork, stop up, plug, plug up
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *asstuppāre, from ad- + *stuppāre, from Latin stuppa. Compare Aromanian astup, astupari, Albanian shtupoj; cf. Sicilian stuppari, attuppari, Venetan stupar, Romansh stuppar, Italian stoppare, French étouper, Old Spanish estopar.

parole.significato: to calm down, be at ease
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *extemperāre, from Latin temperāre.

parole.significato: so (to this or that extent), so much
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum tantum, from Latin eccum + tantum. (The initial syllable of *eccum- compounds regularly turns to /a-/ in Romanian.) Closely parallel to Italian cotanto and Old Catalan aitant. Compare also Old French itant, Old Spanish atanto (as well as French tant, Italian tanto,

parole.significato: au (modal auxiliary, third-person plural form of avea, used with past participles to form perfect compus tenses)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *habunt, as a conjugated form of Latin habeō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad-hacce (from Latin hac) or Latin *ad-hocce (from Latin hoc). Compare Aromanian aoatsi.

Probably from auș (“old man”) + diminutive suffix -el. Other ideas suggest Vulgar Latin aucellus (“small bird”) (compare Italian uccello, French oiseau), from Latin avis, but this is harder to explain due to phonetic difficulties as well as the reason why a general term for bird would apply to a spe
Past participle of avea. From Vulgar Latin *habūtus, replacing Classical Latin habitus.
From Vulgar Latin habessim, from Latin habuissem. Compare Italian avessi, French eusse.
From a Vulgar Latin root *astectāre, from an alteration of Latin adspectāre, an alternative form of aspectāre. Compare Aromanian ashteptu, Italian aspettare, Sardinian aisetare, Sicilian astittari.
Presumably from a Vulgar Latin *eatis, from Latin habēbātis.

parole.significato: to lie in wait for someone by following them closely; lurk behind someone; stalk
parole.testo: From the variant form aținea, from Vulgar Latin *attenēre, from Latin attinēre.

parole.significato: to doze, snooze, begin to fall asleep
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *attepīre, *adtepīre, from Latin tepere (“be warm, tepid”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *baiula, from Latin baiulus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *baba. Compare French bave, Italian bava, Spanish and Portuguese baba. The normal result, *ba, is not used as the singular has been replaced with bală through analogy.

From a contracted Vulgar Latin form (possibly *beb(e)tus) of Late Latin bibitus (“drunk”), from Latin bibō (“drink”). Compare Spanish beodo. Doublet of băut ("beat" probably being of Transylvanian origin).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *verucata, from Latin verruca. Often considered to be from Serbo-Croatian berikat, but this word is instead probably derived from Romanian. If so, doublet of oraș.

parole.significato: a blister, sore, or pustule on the tongue
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *vescella, from a contraction of *vessicella, diminutive of *vessīca, from Latin vēsīca. Cf. also vēsīcula.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs. Equivalent to bou + -ar. Compare Aromanian buyear, French bouvier, Italian boaro, Portuguese boieiro, Spanish boyero.
From an older form *băteza, from Vulgar Latin baptidiāre, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō, “immerse, baptize”).

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *brosca, from broscus (compare Medieval Latin bruscus), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *frosk. Compare Aromanian broascã. Compare also Albanian breshkë, Old French bruesche, Italian rospo, Milanese Lombard brosco, Ladin rusk.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *brothācus, from Ancient Greek βροτάχος (brotákhos), from βάτραχος (bátrakhos). Compare Aromanian broatic, Albanian bretk, bretkosë.

parole.significato: November (eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Formed from brumă + ar, or inherited from Vulgar Latin brūmārius (compare Friulian brumâr (“winter”); cf. also French Brumaire, Albanian brymës (“November”)), from Latin brūma (“winter, mist”) (compare Romanian brumă (“frost”)).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buccata, from Latin bucca. Compare French bouchée, Italian boccata, Portuguese and Spanish bocado. Doublet of bușeu.

parole.significato: with swollen or puffed up cheeks
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *buccidus, from Latin bucca.

Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *umbulita (“small navel”), clipped from Vulgar Latin *umbulicus, from Latin umbilīcus (“navel”), with [um] being reanalyzed as the feminine indefinite article o at some stage as same is evidenced by related Romanian buric. The latter may have provoked such analogy. On groun

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *bot(t)um, *bottia (“bump”) + -uc, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). Compare bot.

parole.significato: To care for or feed an infant.
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *baiāre, from Latin baiulāre (“to carry a burden”). The sense was likely reinterpreted as "to bear a pregnancy" and then "to raise/care for a child." Compare Italian balia.

Inherited from a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vetrānus, syncopated form of Latin veterānus. Compare Aromanian bitãrnu, Vegliot Dalmatian vetrun, Friulian vedran, Old Venetan vetrano. Compare the borrowed veteran.
Unknown. Possibly of imitative origin, or tied to Vulgar Latin baubulāre < Latin baubor, baubari. Compare Campidanese Sardinian baulài, Piedmontese baolè.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bibitūra, from Latin bibitus, from bibō (“drink”). Compare Aromanian biuturã, Sardinian bibidura, bidura.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vissīna, from Latin vissīre. Compare Aromanian bishinã, Megleno-Romanian bișǫnă.
From a Vulgar Latin root *caiulus or *calerus, from Latin galērus.

parole.significato: shaft of a knee-high boot (the upper part that extends from the ankle to the knee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *calamulus, from Latin calamus, from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Compare Spanish carámbano.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cinusia, from Latin cinus, a less common variant of cinis (“ashes”), from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”). Compare Aromanian cinushi.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin citera, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Compare Italian cetra. Doublet of chitară (from Italian), țiteră (from German); cf. also the related citolă (from French).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *clagum, from metathesis of Latin coāgulum (cf. the contracted Late Latin form quaglum, found in some manuscripts). Cognate with Aromanian cljag. A late Eastern Romance (or earlier Romanian) form was borrowed into Ukrainian ґляґ (gljag), dialectal Polish klag, dialec
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *clautoria, from *clautus, from clavutus, ultimately from Latin clāvus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quene, from Latin quem, accusative singular of quī, from Old Latin quei, from Proto-Italic *kʷoi, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos. Compare Aromanian tsini, Sardinian chíne, Spanish quien, Dalmatian ci.

parole.significato: inflorescence (cluster of flowers arranged on a stem)
parole.testo: Unknown. There are several etymologies proposed, and no single one can be said to be far ahead of the others in terms of getting majority preference yet. Pușcariu and Densușianu proposed a derivation from a Vulgar Latin root *circ[u]lina, from Latin circulus, with an Italian dialectal word as the ma

Inherited from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), and ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ceresius, from Late Latin cerasius, from Latin cerasus, from Ancient Greek κέρασος (kérasos). Compare Aromanian ciresh, tsiresh.

parole.significato: June (sixth month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cerasiārium (“June”). By surface analysis, cireașă (“cherry”) + -ar. Compare Aromanian Cirishar
From Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc. Related to Portuguese cá, Spanish acá, French çà.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin cōda, variant of Latin cauda. Compare Aromanian coadã / code.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere.

parole.significato: white-tailed; having a white or light-colored tail and darker body
parole.testo: From coadă (“tail”) + alb (“white”), or possibly from a common Romance or Vulgar Latin source; compare Aromanian cudalbã, Sardinian codalbola.

From a Vulgar Latin *codabattula, from Latin coda < cauda (“tail”) + a derivative of battuō (“to beat”). Compare Aromanian coadã-baturã, cudubaturã, cutrubatã, Calabrese codivattula. See also similar formations in other Romance languages, with inverse order: Italian batticoda, Florentine dialect bat
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *codrum, possibly from a variant of Latin quadrum (“square”) and Latin quadra (“morsel”). Compare Aromanian codru, Albanian kodër.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōleum n, from Latin cōleus m, of Ancient Greek origin. Compare Aromanian colj, coalji.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *colastra, from Latin colostra, colostrum.
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin frequentative root *complexīre, from Latin complexus, or simply an expressive creation.
From credință + -os, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *crēdentiōsus, from crēdentia, from Latin crēdens.
Most likely from crește with the suffix -et. Less likely from creastă or a Vulgar Latin root *cristidum. Compare Aromanian creashtit.
From a Vulgar Latin root *conquerīre or conquaerere, from Latin conquīrere.

parole.significato: bump, swelling (such as that from being hit hard on the head)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *cucullium, from Latin cucullum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *cucūta, from Latin cicūta, of Proto-Indo-European origin.

parole.significato: to immerse, dip, submerge, sink into
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnfundāre, from Latin cōnfundō, cōnfundere, from fundus (“bottom”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clubium, from Ancient Greek κλυβίον (klubíon). Compare Aromanian cuib.

parole.significato: to receive (or give) the Eucharist, Holy Communion
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *comminicāre, from Latin communicāre. Doublet of the borrowed comunica.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *complīre, from Latin complēre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”). Ultimately from cum (“with”) + parō (“prepare”). Compare Italian comprare, Spanish comprar, Aromanian acumpãr, acupãr.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *compitāre (“count, reckon”, root), modified from Latin computāre. Doublet of computa, borrowed from Latin, and conta, borrowed through Italian and French.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coctōrium (“casserole, pan”), probably from Latin coctor (“cook”), from coquō. Compare also Albanian koftor, Italian cottoio, Catalan cuitor.

From Vulgar Latin circus bibit (literally “ring that drinks”), from bibere (“to drink”), late variant of arcus bibit (“rainbow”) (also crās pluit); compare Franco-Provençal arcboit, arboè, Ladin arcobuàn, Neapolitan arcovevere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coliclus < coliculus, from Latin cauliculus. Compare Italian colecchio, Spanish colleja.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōnsutūra, from Latin cōnsuō. By surface analysis, cusut + -ură.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum tālis. Compare Old Catalan aital, Italian cotale.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin cottizāre or cottidiāre (compare Aromanian cutedz, cutidzari, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian cutez, Venetan scotezàr, Istriot cutisà, Aquileian scuttia, compare also Albanian kuxoj), from Ancient Greek κοττίζω (kottízō, “to play craps, shoot dice”).

From a Vulgar Latin root *contremulāre, from Late Latin tremulāre, from Latin tremulus (“trembling”), from tremere (“shake, tremble”). Equivalent to cu- + tremura. Compare Aromanian cutreambur, cutrimburari.

From the variant form cârnaț, subsequently reanalyzed as the plural, thus rendering the current form. From a Vulgar Latin *carnaceum or *carnācius, ultimately from Latin carnis, carō (“meat”). Compare Megleno-Romanian cărnat, Sicilian carnazzu, Spanish carnaza, carniza, Old Occitan carnaza, Portugue
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *caldūra, from Latin caldus, calidus. Compare Italian caldura, Aromanian cãldurã. By surface analysis, cald + -ură.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitāre, from Latin caput. Compare Italian capitare (“happen; turn up, occur; end up”); compare also Albanian kaptoj, cf. Occitan acaptar.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *carrāre, from Latin carrus. Compare Sardinian carrare. Other Romance cognates seem to have come from a root *carriāre. Related through French to English carry.

parole.significato: spot or mark left on the body from sweat, filth, or dirt
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carōnia, ultimately from Latin carō, perhaps influenced in Romanian by râie.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cascāre, from Ancient Greek χάσκω (kháskō, “to yawn, gape”). Compare Aromanian hascu, cascu, Sardinian cascare, cascai.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *cascabundus, from *cascare, or a variation of *căscăun, from căsca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadūtus, past participle for Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *occāsionāre (possibly later changed into a form *cāssionāre, or *accāsionāre), from Latin occāsiō. Compare Italian cagionare, accagionare, Old French achoisoner (however, these may also be internally derived or formed from nouns descending from occāsiō (cf. Italian cagio

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *debtoriu < *dēbitōrius for Latin dēbitor (“debtor”), ultimately from dēbitum (“debt”), from dēbeō (“to owe”); influenced by the verb da (“to give”). Compare Aromanian dãtor. Doublet of the borrowing debitor.
From Old Romanian de + cinde, the latter from Vulgar Latin *eccum inde, whence also Italian quindi.
From a Vulgar Latin root *dedāre, from Latin dēdere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *degelāre, from dē- + gelāre. Compare Aromanian dzeadzir, dzidzirari.

parole.significato: to reel on/up, wind a hank of something on a reel or bobbin
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *depānāre or *depēnāre, from Latin pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos). Compare Aromanian deapin, dipinari, Italian dipanare, Catalan debanar, Spanish devanar, Portuguese dobar, Sardinian demanare.

parole.significato: to tidy up (a house, room etc.)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *dēradicāre, from Latin dē- + radicāre (“take root”) (cf. ridica).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin de ipsa de nocte.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *disclāvāre or *disclāviāre (probably influenced by încheia or cheie), from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus. Compare Aromanian dishcljiedz, dishcljiari; cf. also Friulian disclavâ, French déclouer.
From a Vulgar Latin root *discuneāre, from Latin cuneō, from cuneus.
From des- + încurca, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *de-obscuricare, from Latin obscurus.

parole.significato: to charm away or heal with magic words, such as an illness, or to undo or remove a spell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discantāre, from Latin dis- + cantō. Compare Aromanian discãntu, discãntari, Friulian discjantâ (“disenchant, awaken, make wiser”), Venetan descantar (“wake up, sharpen up”); cf. also French déchanter.

parole.significato: to get off a horse, dismount, alight
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *discaballicāre, from dis- + Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus (“horse”). Compare Aromanian discalic, discãlicari or Albanian shkalkoj. Sense 2 may have been influenced by a migratory or nomadic Central Asian people that entered lands occupied by Romanians, as a

Unknown. One proposed etymology was a Vulgar Latin *disfabicāre. It is more likely linked to or derived from Romanian înșfăca. Cf. also Aromanian dizvoc, dizvucari (“tear to shreds, delapidate, wreck”), which may or may not be related. See also the rare and dialectal Romanian dezvoca, which may be a
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *disglaciāre, from dis- + glaciāre. Compare Aromanian dizgljets, dizgljitsari.

parole.significato: to shell (remove outer covering or shell), husk (remove husks from), pod (remove peas from their pod), shuck.
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *disglubicāre or alternatively composed of dez- + ghioc + -a.

parole.significato: to wake up from a state such as that of drunkenness, stupor, fear, powerful emotion, or dizziness; sober up
parole.testo: Unknown. One possibility may be a Vulgar Latin root *dismatticāre, from Latin mattus (“drunk”). Another etymology may be from an earlier form *desmântici, from a Latin root *de-exmenticāre, with change of conjugation (compare Italian dimenticare). Compare the verb dezmeți, and also dezmetic, possibl

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dismerdāre, a verb based on Latin merda (“faeces”). The sense evolution from "remove faeces" to "caress" appears to have occurred in the context of childcare. Compare Aromanian diznjerdu.

parole.significato: to live unrestrained, licentiously or in libertinage
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *dismētiāre, from dis- + Latin metīrī. Compare Spanish desmedirse (“to overstep the mark”).

parole.significato: to unlearn, become unfamiliar with, forget how to do something, wean from, stop or break off a habit
parole.testo: From dez- + învăța, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *disvitiāre, from *vitiāre (in the sense of "accustom, habituate, familiarize"), from Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Aromanian dizvets, dizvitsari, cf. also Italian divezzare, svezzare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin diserrāre, from dis- + serrāre. Alternatively, related to șir.

parole.significato: to awaken, to wake up, to rouse
parole.testo: Traditionally considered to be from Vulgar Latin *deexcitāre, from Latin de- + excitāre (“wake up”) (cf. Italian destare, also Dalmatian destruar), but is more likely from Latin dispectāre (frequentative of dispiciō (“look, discern, perceive, discover”) through its past participle dispectus). It is

From a Vulgar Latin *duī (“two”, root), from Latin duo, probably formed through analogy with the usual nominative masculine plural ending in -ī. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. The similar formation of *duī also happened in Old French dui, nominative form of deus.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. This is the original and now dated Romanian word for the back - mainly replaced in common usage by the (originally popular, now standard language) alternative spate (“back”). Compare French dos and Romansh dies.
From an earlier *drepănea, from a Vulgar Latin root *drepanella, diminutive of Latin drepanis.

From a Vulgar Latin root *doliōsus, ultimately from Latin dolor or dolēre. Compare Italian doglioso, Friulian duliôs. Also possibly from an unattested, lost Romanian word *doi, from Vulgar Latin *dolium, from Latin cordolium.

parole.significato: to tear, usually to drop into a liquid (milk, stew)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *dēmīcāre, from Latin mīca. Compare Aromanian dinjic, dinjicari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post. Compare Aromanian dupã, Italian dopo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Italian diramare, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

parole.significato: to tire, tire out, wear out, exhaust, overfatigue
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *derenēre or *derenāre, from Latin rēn (“kidney”). Compare Italian direnare, Spanish derrengar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *illus, from Latin ille.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *facla, from a contraction of Latin facula (“little torch”), from fax (“torch”). Doublet of făclie and faclă (borrowings through Slavic and Greek intermediates), and flacără (from a Vulgar Latin variant form).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *favulus, from Latin favus, or taken from faguri, plural of fag, an older form of the word.
From the plural of famăn, from Vulgar Latin (homo) *feminus, from Latin femina. Compare Aromanian feamin. Compare Portuguese fêmeo, Old Occitan feme.
From a Vulgar Latin *fetiola, a diminutive of Latin feta, from fetus.

parole.significato: youth, boy, child, unmarried young man
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *fētiolus, from Latin fetus. Compare Aromanian ficior.
From farmec or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *pharmacāre, from Latin pharmacum.

parole.significato: to boil (heat (a liquid) until it begins to turn into a gas)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fervere < Classical Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeru- (“to be hot, boil”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n. Compare Aromanian heari.

Past participle of fierbe. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fertus, contraction of *fervitus for the past participle of Latin ferveō, fervere, as with the Aromanian equivalent hertu. Compare also Apulian (dialect of Italy) fiersetu.

parole.significato: many pieces of iron or instruments made from iron
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *ferratalia, from Latin ferrum. Compare Portuguese ferratalha.
From the verb fi + -ință. Also, possibly based on a Vulgar Latin root *fientia (from the Latin verb fiō), a popular equivalent of Latin essentia. Compare Aromanian hiintsã.

parole.significato: a part of the underside of a yoke
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *fībulāria, ultimately from Latin fībula.
From a Vulgar Latin root *florilia, from Latin Flōrālia, from Flōra (“goddess of flowers”), from flōs (“flower”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin forficāre, ultimately from Latin forfex (“scissors”). Compare Aromanian nfoarfic, nfurficari, furtichedz, Sardinian forfigare, Asturian aforfegar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, metathesis of Late Latin fimbria (“fringe, border, edge”), from Latin fimbriae. Compare French frange.
From a Vulgar Latin root *frānctus, from Latin frāctus. Compare Aromanian frãmtu, Italian franto, Friulian frant.

Inherited from Latin frāctura through a Vulgar Latin root *franctura (cf. also Old French frainture, Old Italian frantura), or from frânt + -ură, past participle of frânge. Compare fractură, a borrowed doublet.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Compare Italian fuggire, French fuir, Portuguese fugir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *fulger, from Latin fulgur (“lightning”), from Proto-Italic *folgos.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fulgerāre, from Latin fulgurāre.
Probably from a variant of fumuriu. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *fūmulus, from Latin fūmus.

parole.significato: gossamer (strand of cobweb floating in the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *fūnicellus, diminutive of Latin fūnis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūrāre, from Latin fūror.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Italian formicaio, Portuguese formigueiro, Spanish hormiguero, Catalan formiguer, Friulian furmiâr.

From a Vulgar Latin root *furuncellus, from Latin furunculus, possibly later influenced by the furnica in Romanian. Compare Aromanian furuntsel, furnitsel. Doublet of the neological borrowing furuncul.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fusticellus, diminutive of Latin fustis.
From a Vulgar Latin root *fenacium or *fenaceum, from Latin fenum, or a back-formation from fânețe, plural of fâneață. Cf. also French fenasse, Catalan and Occitan fenàs, fenassa.

parole.significato: to knock, break, smash, or dash to pieces/smithereens; to crumble
parole.testo: Aphetic form of variant sfărâma, verbal derivative of sfărâmă, older variant of fărâmă (“piece, crumb”). Other theories start from the variant form sfărâma, sfărma, deriving from a Vulgar Latin root *exformāre (compare Italian sformare). See also înfărma. Compare Aromanian sãrmu, Albanian thërrmoj.

From a Vulgar Latin root *cavula, diminutive of Late Latin cava, from Latin cavus, cavum, or reformed through *găuri, the plural of a hypothetical earlier Romanian *gău, from cavus. Cf. zgău. Compare also Aromanian gavrã; cf. Albanian gavër.
From a Vulgar Latin root *genna, from Latin gena, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus (“chin, jaw, cheek”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/-a, from Latin glaciēs.
From the form gheabă, from Vulgar Latin *glibba, through metathesis from *gibbla, contracted form of gibbula (word used by Vegetius), from Latin gibbus.

parole.significato: bar on a window or doorway that forms part of a screen, grill or grating when aligned horizontally and vertically
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *gratis, from Latin crātis.
From a Vulgar Latin root *graulus or *gravulus, from Latin graculus (“jackdaw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare French grolle, Italian gravolo.

parole.significato: nausea (feeling of physical unwellness, usually with the desire to vomit)
parole.testo: From greu + -eață. Other theories include a Vulgar Latin root *gravities or *grevitia, ultimately from Latin gravis. Compare Aromanian greatsã.

From grec + -esc. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *graeciscus or Old Church Slavonic грьчьскъ (grĭčĭskŭ). Compare Aromanian gãrtsescu/grãtsescu, Old French grezois, and Russian греческий (grečeskij).

From a Vulgar Latin root *grylliolus, from Latin gryllus, from Ancient Greek γρύλλος (grúllos, “performer in an Egyptian dance, comic figure, caricature”). The Vulgar Latin form would have normally yielded Romanian *greior initially, followed by later changes; another more likely explanation starts
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grevitātem, from Latin gravitās, gravitātem (thus a doublet of the borrowing gravitate). By surface analysis, greu + -tate.

parole.significato: a piglet of about one year of age
parole.testo: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *groscellu < *grossicellus from Latin grossus + the diminutive suffix -(ic)ellus. It may have been formed from the plural of an original singular form *groștel.
From gras or possibly Vulgar Latin *grassōnem.

parole.significato: grain (harvested seeds of various grass-related food crops), corn
parole.testo: Remade analogically as a singular from the original form grăunț (later interpreted as a plural), itself from an alteration of an earlier *grănuț with a nasal infix, from Vulgar Latin root *granuceum or *granutium, ultimately from Latin grānum. Compare Aromanian gãrnuts.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *gutturālium, from Latin gutturālia, plural of gutturālis, from guttur. The variant gutunar was probably influenced by Serbian.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gusia (compare Aromanian gushi, gushe, Albanian gushë, Italian gozzo (“gizzard”), Friulian gose, French gosier (“gullet”)), from Late Latin geusiae, from Gaulish geusiae (compare Welsh gewai (“glutton”)).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gamphae, from Ancient Greek γαμφαί (gamphaí), variation of γαμφηλαί (gamphēlaí, “jaw of an animal”).
Unknown. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *era. Compare Engadine Romansh eir, Provençal er, era, Old Galician-Portuguese ar (“also, again”).
From iarnă + -atic. Possibly also linked to Vulgar Latin hibernaticum (attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin hibernum; compare French hivernage. Compare Aromanian arnatic.
From ierta + -ciune, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *lībertātiō, *lībertātiōnem, from Latin lībertō. Compare Aromanian ljirtãciuni.
A variant use of îns (before the mid 19th century it was pronounced the same), from Vulgar Latin *ipsus, from Latin ipse.

parole.significato: a large, tall, or high chair, similar to a throne
parole.testo: Various theories exist. Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *iacium or *jacium, from Latin iaceō (“to lie, recline”); compare Italian giaccio (“pen for sheep”) (Italian diaccio and addiaccio) and Sicilian jazzu (“burrow; bed”). The etymology traditionally and most commonly given is German Sitz (“seat”
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iugastrum.
From junghia + -tură, perhaps representing a Vulgar Latin *juglatūra < *iugulatūra, from Latin iugulatūrus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasou.

Unknown. One theory proposes a Vulgar Latin *laesionāre, from Latin laesiō (“harm, injury”), with an original Romanian form presumably *leșuna (as with cășuna, mișuna, etc.), undergoing a change later (compare also tușina). Cf. also Latin lassō, lassāre ("to faint"). Another possibility is that it m
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lenus, from Latin lenis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *landīcus, from Latin landīca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūcōrem, from Latin lūceō. Equivalent to luci + -oare. Compare Italian lucore, French lueur, Catalan llugor, Occitan lugor.
From lung. Also possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *longīre for Latin longīscēre.
From lung + -ime, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *longimen, from Latin longus. Compare Aromanian lundzimi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin lacusta, alteration of Latin locusta, of uncertain origin. Doublet of langustă, which was borrowed from French.
Plural of lătură, itself from a Vulgar Latin root *lavatūra (plural *lavaturae), from Latin lavō. Compare Italian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, French lavure.

Probably linked to the verb la. Possibly from Vulgar Latin root *lavōnem (“washhouse”), from Latin lavō or with the creative suffix -un. Another less likely theory suggests Latin leōnem, from leō (see leu). See also Lăunele, the name of a river in Oltenia, Romania.
From lat; also possibly from a Vulgar Latin *latīre, from Latin latēscere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mixticāre, derived from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Compare Aromanian misticari, Dalmatian mescur.

Supposedly from Vulgar Latin *miccus, from Doric Greek μῑκκός (mīkkós, “small”), variant of μικρός (mikrós). Compare Aromanian njic, Extreme Southern Italian nicu and miccu, Corsican micca, also Italian miccino. May also be related to Latin mīca (“crumb”); compare mică.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n. Compare Aromanian njari.
From a Vulgar Latin root *messionāre, from Latin messiō.

parole.significato: a tuft of wool or hair
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *agnicia, from *agnicius (“of lamb”), from Latin agnus (“lamb”). Compare Aromanian njitsã.

parole.significato: thaw (warmer, humid weather following the cold of winter; warmth of weather sufficient to melt that which is frozen)
parole.testo: Related to or derived from moale (plural moi), or from muia, with the suffix -ină. Other attempts have been made to link it to a derivative of Vulgar Latin *mollināre (cf. the verb moina), or from *mollimen, or *molliō, molliōnis, or to a lost early Romanian *moiu, from Latin root *mollius. One theo
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *muccicālium, from Latin muccidus, the same source as muced (“moldy, fusty”). Formed similarly to putregai. Compare Italian moccicaglia.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *mut(i)la, from *mutilus, alteration of Latin mutulus. Another alternative may be ultimately from cumulus, possibly crossed with mutulus or transposed into a form *muc(u)lus, and changed to feminine gender. Compare Aromanian muclji, Italian mucchio.

parole.significato: synonym of înmuia (“to soften; to dip”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *molliāre, derived from Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Aromanian muljari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mŭlgĕre, from Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin mora, from Latin morum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron). Compare Italian mora, French mûre, Catalan móra, Spanish mora.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūsclus, syncopated form of Latin mūsculus (“muscle”), from mūs (“mouse”). Compare Aromanian mushclju.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūsclus, syncopated form of *mūsculus, diminutive of Latin mūscus (“moss”). Compare Italian muschio, Venetan muscio, Friulian muscli, Aromanian mushclju.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin musaroneus, from musaraneus (“shrew”). Compare Aromanian mushuronjiu (“mole”), Italian musaragno (“shrew”), French mûrègne (“anthill”), Venetan musiga (“mole”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manucāre, from Latin manducāre. Compare Italian manucare, variant of manducare, itself an obsolete variant of mangiare (this form being a borrowing from French).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manganeāre or *manganiāre, from Ancient Greek μαγγανεύω (manganeúō); see μάγγανον (mánganon, “charm”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mana, from Latin manus f. Compare Aromanian mãnã, Megleno-Romanian mǫnă, Istro-Romanian măre, Italian and Neapolitan mana. The rest of Romance retains the original Latin form (cf. Italian mano).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mēlus, from Latin mālus. Compare Italian melo.

parole.significato: great, splendid, magnificent, grand, grandiose, stately, imposing
parole.testo: From mare + -eț or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *maricius, from Latin mas, marem.

Unknown; often considered to be from a Vulgar Latin *marracīna, *marrūcīna, [Term?] derived from Latin marra (“thorn”), but possibly also from an alteration of Latin malitia, with the influence of the Romanian suffix -ciune. Compare Spanish maleza. Compare also the related Albanian mërqinje, with th
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *metula, see which for more. Compare Albanian nétull.
From Vulgar Latin *mita, from Latin amita by aphaeresis, with -ușă (diminutive suffix) added later in Romanian.
From Vulgar Latin nīs, from Latin nos. Compare nă (old form) and Aromanian nã.
Unknown. Probably an expressive creation. See râncheza. An alternate etymology proposed is a Vulgar Latin *hinnutulāre (from Latin hinnus), later influenced by râncheza.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *nescio quene, from Latin nesciō quem, accusative singular of quī.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nemīca, from ne- + mīca. Compare Old French ne ... mie, Old Venetan nemiga. Compare also Italian mica.
From nară, with the suffix -tos instead of -os, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *nāritōsus, from Latin nāris. Cf. also nărtilă.

Past participle of naște. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *nāscūtus, from Latin nāscor. Compare Aromanian nãscut, Catalan and Occitan nascut, Dalmatian nascoit, Friulian nassût, Ladin nascù, Romansh naschiu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ōvāria, from Latin ovum, or less likely *avula.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus, from Proto-Italic *okelos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Compare Italian occhio. Doublet of oculus, borrowed through French.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ossāmen, derived from Latin os.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plātinus, from Latin platanus (“plane tree”), itself from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos); same change of meaning in Albanian panjë (“sycamore maple”). See also Romanian platan, an etymological doublet stemming from the same Greek word.

parole.significato: an offering or dole made for the dead at a funeral (in the form of wine mixed with honey and water sprinkled on the bod…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pausum, from Latin pausō.

parole.significato: rush, bulrush, club-rush, cattail, reed mace (Typha)
parole.testo: Inherited from a Vulgar Latin *papura, from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of papir and papirus. Compare Megleno-Romanian papră.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, re-analysed as a feminine singular.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pertrāicere, from Latin per- + trāicere. Compare Aromanian pitrec, pitreatsiri.

parole.significato: to propose, ask to marry, often through an intermediate, such as the woman's family
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere (“ask, request”). Compare Italian pezzire, Spanish pedir.

Uncertain, maybe from the root *peh₂w- (“few, small”). Most likely from Vulgar Latin picca, from earlier *piccus, borrowed from Proto-Celtic *bikkos (“small, little”). Eventually influenced by dissimilation by paucus (“few, little”). Compare Albanian pikë (“a drop; a bit”), Sicilian picca (“a bit, a

parole.significato: thrums, all the remaining unwoven threads that are cut from the warp of a fabric
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *pedinus, from Latin pes, pedis. Compare Aromanian cheadin, Albanian pedim, Italian penero, pedano, pedene, Sicilian pèdinu, pèdanu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *pīsāre, from Latin pīnsāre; compare Aromanian chisedz, chisari. Akin to Spanish pisar and Portuguese pisar.

parole.significato: a wooden or metal vessel which is used for the grinding of various things; mortar
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pilla, from Latin pīla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, of echoic origin. Compare Aromanian chishair, chish.

parole.significato: plateau; flat raised area or expanse of terrain
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plagium, ultimately from Ancient Greek πλάγιος (plágios). Compare Albanian pllajë. Compare Latin plagia, whence came Italian spiaggia / piaggia, French plage (and the borrowed Romanian doublet of plajă (“beach”)), Spanish playa, Portuguese praia.

parole.significato: a floating islet made of decaying grass, reeds, bent, or driftwood
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin root *plabulum, from Latin pābulum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plŏ(v)ia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ploppus, from classical Latin pōpulus. Compare Italian pioppo.

parole.significato: to rain (of rain: to fall from the sky)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere, with a later change to the first conjugation type within Romanian or reformed based on the original subjunctive (pluat). Compare Aromanian ploai, Corsican piova.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palpabundus, from Latin palpāre, or palpandus.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *plausāre, from plausus.

parole.significato: partridge (a bird of the genera Perdix or Alectoris)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *peturnīcula, from a blend of Latin perdix and coturnix, with the suffix -cula. Compare Aromanian pitruniclji. The oldest attested form may be пътꙋᵖɴике (/pəturˈnike/ or in modernised spelling păturniche), found as a surname in a document from Suceava dated to 1597. For t
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *prigitāre, from Late Latin pīgritārī, from Latin pīgrō. Less likely from a root *prae-agitāre < prae + agitāre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin preb(i)ter or prev(i)ter, popular variant of Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare Albanian prift, Aromanian preftu, preft, Italian prete, French prêtre, Catalan prevere. Doublet of prezbiter.
From a Vulgar Latin *pervescīre or *perviescere, from Latin viēscere (“wither”), from vieō.

parole.significato: to look after, guard, watch over (especially a dead body before burial, for a wake)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *perviglāre, from Latin pervigilāre.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pueruncus, from Latin puer (“child”) + diminutive suffix -unculus. In Balkan Latin, a popular, syncopated variant of the suffix -unculus was *-unclus, hence words like unchi, rărunchi, genunchi, etc. This *puerunclus was hypercorrected by analogy with Latin iuvencus ("ca
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neuter plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).

parole.significato: to plunder, pillage, sack, rob, loot, ravage, ransack
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *praedāre, from Latin praedārī.

Probably from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of Latin pullus (“offspring, child, cub, chick, etc.”). Compare Aromanian pulã, Catalan and Spanish polla, also Dalmatian pula. An alternate, and less likely, etymology derives it from a Vulgar Latin root *pūbula, from pūbes.

From a Vulgar Latin *puppāre, from puppa (“breast, teat, nipple”), from Latin pūpa; or perhaps formed from a hypothetical, now lost noun *pupă in early Romanian, from this Latin word. Compare Italian poppare (“to suckle”), poppa (“boob, breast”), Catalan and Occitan popar (“to suckle”), popa (“boob,

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *pūlicāre, from Latin pūlex, pūlicem. Compare Aromanian puric, puricari, Logudorese puligare, Sardinian pulicare. Superficially, and semantically, resembles Vulgar Latin *pilūc(i)cāre and its reflexes.

parole.significato: to be able to; can, could, may
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse.
From putea (“be able to”) + -re; from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse (“can, be able to”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *putricālium, from Latin putridus, the same source as putred (“rotten”). Formed similarly to mucegai.

parole.significato: a blister, sore, or pustule in the mouth, particularly on the tongue
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *pustulella, diminutive from Latin pustula. The early loss of the second /u/, and then change of /tl/ to /kl/, are regular.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *putīre, from Latin putēre.

Uncertain, as with a number of similar words across the Romance languages. Probably from Vulgar Latin *putīnus, a blend/alteration of Latin pisinnus, pittinnus and putillus, pusillus, all meaning “a teeny boy”. Compare Aromanian putsãn; further Albanian picërr, Italian piccino and piccolo, French pe
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pergla, from Latin pergula, with the meaning of a stall outside of a hut or a support for vines changing to that of a small girder or beam.

parole.significato: fuzz, lint, fluff; flock (coarse tuft of wool)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pettia, from Late Latin pettia. Compare Albanian pjesë, French pièce, Spanish pieza, Catalan and Portuguese peça, Italian pezza, pezzo.

From an unattested early Romanian singular form *păresimă, though a derivative is attested; părăsimă. From Vulgar Latin *quaresima, from Latin quadrāgēsima (“the fortieth part; Lent”), substantive of quadrāgēsimus (“fortieth”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palanga, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx). Compare Italian and Spanish palanca, French planche. Doublet of palancă and falangă.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum (“weight”).

parole.significato: to go, to leave, to walk, to pass
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun). See also the neologism pasa, a doublet borrowed from French.

Most likely from Vulgar Latin *pistālia, from Latin pistāre, from pinsō (“stamp, pound, crush”); also hypothesized to be (due to the -aie ending) from various other possible Latin sources, including *quassitālia, from quassāre, or *pyxitālia, from pyxis. Compare Albanian bishtajë and Aromanian pãsta

Probably from Vulgar Latin *pictāre, a verb based on Classical Latin pictus (“painted”). For the semantics, cf. Spanish pinta (“stain”) < pintar (“paint”, verb). The normal outcome of /kt/ is /pt/ in Romanian, but the loss of /p/ in this case can be explained as the result of dissimilation from the
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patubulum, from Latin patibulum (“crossbeam”).
Either from Vulgar Latin *pittula, diminutive of *pitta, or from paturi, the plural of pat ("bed").

parole.significato: to have something, chiefly negative or sometimes neutral, happen to oneself
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin ragĕre. Compare French raire, réer; cf. also French railler, Italian ragliare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *radia, from Latin radius. Doublet of radius. Compare Spanish raza.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *repausum, from Latin repausō. Compare Aromanian arãpas, Italian riposo, French repos, Catalan repòs, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso.
From a Vulgar Latin root *retella, a diminutive of Latin rēte, retis. Compare Abruzzo Italian dialect ritedda, compare also French réseau.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *reniclus, from Latin rēniculus (“little kidney”), from rēnēs (“kidneys”), from ren. Compare Aromanian arniclju, Sardinian arrigu.

parole.significato: a deforested area used for pasture or cultivation
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *runcus, from Latin runcō. Compare Latin runcātio and Italian ronchio.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rhonchizāre (“to snore”) (compare Old Italian roncheggiare, Istriot ronchizea), from Latin rhoncō, rhonchāre (compare Spanish roncar), denominative of rhonchus (“snoring”), from Ancient Greek ῥόγχος (rhónkhos).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hirundinella, diminutive of classical Latin hirundō, hirundine. Compare also French hirondelle.
From rândunea + -ică, from Vulgar Latin *hirundinella, diminutive of classical Latin hirundo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rius (river), from Latin rīvus (“brook, small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós, from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós.

Probably from an earlier form *arăbda(re), from a Vulgar Latin *ēlib(ī)dāre (“to force oneself not to desire”), from Latin ē in privative sense + libīdō, with a later apheresis of the initial a-. Compare Aromanian aravdu, arãvdari. Another theory is that it derives from a Vulgar Latin root *reemendā
Unknown. Probably linked to repede or Vulgar Latin *rapicāre. Also possibly from Vulgar Latin *repicāre (a root), from Latin rēpēns or *repigāre, from Latin rēpō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapere, from Proto-Italic *rapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rp-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
From the form rănunchi, from Vulgar Latin *renunclus < Late Latin rēnunculus (“little kidney”), a diminutive of Latin rēn.
Probably from răs- + coace or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *re-excocere, from re- + ex- + coquere.
Unknown. Usually considered to be from răs- + față (“face”), or derived from a Vulgar Latin root *re-ex-faciare, ultimately from facies. Other theories include an alteration of desfăta.
From Vulgar Latin *resalīre, from Latin re- + salīre. Synchronically derivable from ră- + sări. Compare Aromanian arsar.

parole.significato: to get lost, become lost, lose oneself.
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *erraticīre, from *errāticāre, from Latin errāticus, from errō, errāre.

parole.significato: his/hers (that which is his or hers)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *sa, from Latin sua, the feminine form of suus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin sale, from Latin sāl, salem.

parole.significato: fluffy woolen mantle worn by peasants, especially shepherds in mountain regions
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *sarica, from Latin sērica.

parole.significato: the sensation of being full/satisfied/sated; satiety
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *satium, from Latin satis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre, from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiāre from the older form scâmba. Compare Albanian shkëmbej, Italian scambiare.

parole.significato: to remove, take out, subtract, bring out, pull out, throw out
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excotere, from Latin excutere.

parole.significato: to strain or exert oneself, to push (used especially in the context of the effort of defecation or occasionally of givi…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expremere, from Latin exprimere, possibly influenced by excrementum phonetically. Compare Aromanian mi-sprem, sprimeari, mi-spreamit. Doublet of exprima, borrowed through French.

Probably from an older form *scu(i)pi, from Vulgar Latin root *scupīre, from *escopīre, or *excuppere, from Late Latin *exconspuere, ultimately from Latin conspuere, from spuō. Compare Spanish escupir, Portuguese cuspir. Compare also Aromanian ascuchiu.

parole.significato: to scratch, scrape, poke, disturb the earth or ground, in order to take something out or dig a hole (often of animals)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *excorrimare. Another possibility (perhaps more likely) is a relation to scrum.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excurtus, from Latin curtus (“short”); the initial s- may also have been added later in Romanian, or appeared as a result of the influence of scurta, from excurtare. Compare also Aromanian shcurtu. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excutulāre, from Latin excutere. Compare Aromanian ascutur, ascuturari, Megleno-Romanian scutur, scuturari, Italian scotolare, Tarantino scutulare, Abruzzese scutelà.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scantilia, from Latin scintilla.

parole.significato: to decrease, diminish, shrink, mitigate, reduce
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *excadēre (“fall out”), from Latin ex- + cadere. Compare Aromanian scad, scãdeari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”). Compare Aromanian scap, scãpari.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excarmināre, from Latin ex- + carminō (“to card”), from carmen (“card for wool, flax”). Compare Aromanian scarmin, scãrminari, Calabrese scarminare, Spanish escarmenar, Italian scarmigliare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sicilāre, from Latin sicilis (“sickle”). Compare Aromanian sitsirari.
From s- + fâșie or less likely a Vulgar Latin root *exfasciāre, from Latin fasciāre, from fascia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *senicus, Latin senex.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exmiculare, from *micŭla, derived from Latin mica.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exmŭlgĕre, itself from Latin ex- + mulgēre (“to milk”), or as a variant of ēmulgēre with a change of prefix. Compare Aromanian zmulgu, zmuldziri, Albanian zmolje (“fallow land”), Italian smungere, Venetan smónzer, Asturian esmucir. An alternative past participle, smult (

parole.significato: to sip, suck in, drink in
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorbīre, from Latin sorbēre.

parole.significato: broken, fractured, broken into many pieces
parole.testo: Past participle of sparge. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *sparctus instead of Latin sparsus, or formed through analogy with other similar past participles. Compare also Aromanian aspartu.

Possibly from Vulgar Latin *expa(v)orere or Latin expavēre, from Latin pavor. The exact development or derivation is unclear, however: proposals have included a root *exparere or *expavorāre. Another solution might be *spăurea-> spăria-> speria. Compare Aromanian aspar, aspãreari, Megleno-Romanian s

parole.significato: to rip, split, cleave, rend, cut
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expanticāre (“to burst”) (compare Aromanian spãntic, spãnticari, Venetan spantegar (“to bust; scatter, sprinkle”), Calabrian spantecare (“to open”), Abruzzese spandecà (“annoy, bother, torture”), from Latin pantices (“bowels”), plural of pantex; cf. pântece.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *expulverāre, ultimately from Latin pulvis. Compare Aromanian spulbir, spulbirari and Italian spolverare.
From a Vulgar Latin root *expendiolāre, ultimately from Latin pendere. Compare Aromanian aspindzur, aspindzurari. Compare Italian spenzolare.
From a Vulgar Latin *experlavāre, from Late Latin perlavāre, from Latin lavāre (“wash”). Compare Aromanian spel, aspel, spilari, and also Albanian shpëlaj (“to rinse”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extorcere, ultimately from Latin torquēre. Compare Aromanian astorcu. Doublet of extorca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oestricula, derived from Latin oestrus. Compare Aromanian streclji.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *extracōlāre or *transcōlāre, from Latin cōlāre (“filter, strain, purify”). Compare Aromanian stricor, stricurari. Less likely from s- + trece (“pass”), and with influence from verbs like spânzura, vântura, etc.

parole.significato: to have the unpleasant feeling on the teeth and mouth when eating something sour
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extorpidire, from torpidus (“benumbed”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *strigāre (“scream like a screech owl”) from Latin strix (“screech owl”). Compare Megleno-Romanian strig, strigari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin strabus, from Ancient Greek στρᾰβός (străbós), akin to Aromanian strãmbu, Albanian shtrembër, Italian strambo, Friulian stramp, Spanish zambo.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strinctus, from Latin strictus. Compare Aromanian strimtu. A similar nasal infix occurred in old Italian and Neapolitan strinto, Friulian strent, Venetan strento, Logudorese Sardinian istrintu, French étreint. Doublet of strict, ultimately borrowed from the same source.

parole.significato: a narrow pass or strait, tight or narrow passage, enclosed area
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *strinctura, from Late Latin strictura, from Latin strictus. Doublet of the borrowing strictură.

parole.significato: to pass through go through or over, penetrate, traverse
parole.testo: From stră- + bate, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *extrabattere, from Latin battuere. Compare Aromanian strãbat, strãbatiri.

parole.significato: to shine, to sparkle, to radiate, to glister, to beam, to flare; to be bright
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrālūcīre, from Latin lūcēre. By surface analysis, stră- + luci.

parole.significato: a goad (long pointed stick used to prod animals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *stimulāria, from Latin stimulus (the archaic variant form strămur may derive directly from stimulus). Compare Aromanian strimburari, Megleno-Romanian strămulari.

parole.significato: to shift, change places, dislodge, displace, move
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin root *extrāmūtāre, instead of Latin trānsmūtāre. Equivalent to stră- + muta. Compare Aromanian strãmut, strãmutari, Friulian stramudâ, Sardinian stramudai.
From stră- + nepot or less likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrānepōs, extrānepōtem. Compare also Albanian shtërnip.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *extrāpungere, change of prefix from *trānspungere, from Latin pungere. Compare Aromanian strãpungu, strãpundziri, cf. also Friulian strapongi, Venetan straponzer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *stypus or *stupus, from Ancient Greek στύπος (stúpos, “stem, stump, block”).
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *stupire, formed from a crossing of Vulgar Latin *scupire (compare Romanian scuipa) and Latin spūtō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stirparia, from stirps.

From a Vulgar Latin root *stancus, from a contraction of Vulgar Latin *stānticus (“tired”), from Latin stāns, stantis. Compare Aromanian stãngu, also Old Italian mano stanca (“left hand”); cf. also the etymology of Italian manco (“left; originally 'maimed', 'faulty' 'imperfect'”).

parole.significato: a winter stable for sheep or other animals
parole.testo: Probably from staul n + -ină f; another proposed etymology was a Vulgar Latin *stabulīna f, from Latin stabulum n.
From sub- + braț, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *subbracchium, from Latin sub- + bracchium; compare Galician sobrazo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

From a Vulgar Latin root *sufflitum, from Latin sufflō, from flō (“to breathe”). Compare Aromanian suflit, derived from the same Vulgar Latin root. Compare also the Latin word animus, anima ("soul, also breath") deriving from the Proto-Indo-European root for "to breathe", as well as Latin spiritus (
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *subfronticella, from Latin sub + frontis + diminutive suffix -ella, possibly with influence from cilia. Compare Aromanian sufrãmtseauã, sufrãndzeauã.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūgillum, from Latin sigillum (“seal”) crossed with sūgillāre (“to bruise”). Compare Italian suggello. See also the borrowed doublet sigiliu.

From an earlier hypothetical form *sughiuța, from Vulgar Latin *suggluttiāre, probably from an alteration of Latin singultō, singultāre, from singultus, with the prefix sub-. The (Vulgar) Latin was probably influenced by gluttiō, gluttīre (cf. înghiți). Compare Aromanian sugljits, sugljitsari, Sicil
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sublum, from *sūbulum, from Late Latin insūbulum, from Latin insuō + -bulum, or related to sūbula. Compare Italian subbio.
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *sublicidus, from Latin sublica.
From a Vulgar Latin root *sulfīna, from Latin sulphur, sulfur.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subla, from Latin sūbula, from Proto-Indo-European *syuh₁-dʰleh₂, which consists of the root *syewH- (“sew”) and the suffix *-dʰlom (“tool suffix”).

Related to sănătate. Possibly from Vulgar Latin (herba) sanatōria, from Late Latin sanatōrius, from Latin sanō. This form came to be influenced by the verb suna (cf. sunător) in Romanian, altered through popular etymology deriving it from that verb.

parole.significato: (of women, often in the countryside) good friend; a friendly and familiar term used to address a fellow woman
parole.testo: Probably formed from soră as fârtat was from frate, analogically. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *sororiāta, from a verb sororiāre.
From a gender shift of surcel, from Vulgar Latin surcellus, variant of Latin surculus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin surcellus, variant of Latin surculus.

From a Vulgar Latin root *subrūpāre, from Latin rupes (“cliff”). Compare Aromanian surpu, surpari, old Abruzzese dialect surrupare, Sicilian sdirupari. Compare also Italian dirupare, Galician and Portuguese derrubar, Spanish derribar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *suta, see which for more.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sambata, from Vulgar Latin *sambatum, from Latin sabbatum. The Latin is derived from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton, “Sabbath”), ultimately from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath, Shabbat”). Compare French samedi (“Saturday”), itself also from *sambatī diēs. Compare als
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *summicēlla, from Latin summa.

parole.significato: to wake up in the morning
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *sānicāre, from Latin sānus. Less likely from a root *signicāre (“make the sign of the cross”), referring to one’s morning prayers. Preserved only in popular spells.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, accusative of sanguis. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare Catalan sang, French sang, Italian and Portuguese sangue, Spanish sangre, Aromanian sãndzi, sãndze.

parole.significato: purse or pouch worn around the neck
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *sacculeus, from Latin sacculus. Compare Aromanian sãculj.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sānitōsus, from Latin sānitās + -ōsus. Compare Aromanian sãnãtos, cf. also Albanian shëndoshë.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sappāre, from Latin sappa. Compare Aromanian sap, sãpari, French saper, Italian zappare, Sicilian zappari, Spanish zapar, Friulian sapâ, Venetan sapar.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *salāre, from a change in conjugation of Latin salīre (“to salt”), from sal. Compare Italian salare, French saler, Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan salar, Friulian salâ, also Aromanian ãnsar, ãnsãrari.

parole.significato: ground salt mixed with bran, given to sheep
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *salōnem, from Latin sal (“salt”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *seus or *sous, from Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé (“self”).
From Vulgar Latin *ta, from Latin tua, feminine of tuus.

parole.significato: fear (uncountable: emotion caused by actual or perceived danger or threat)
parole.testo: From the verb teme (“to fear”) or possibly from a Vulgar Latin tima. Compare Italian tema, Romansh tema, temma.

parole.significato: rods over which cloth or canvas are stretched over a surface
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tendicla, syncopated form of Latin tendicula.

From tânăr (“young”) + -ețe, from -eață, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *teneritia, from Latin tener. Compare Aromanian tinireatsã, Italian tenerezza, Old Sicilian tinirizza, Catalan tendresa, French tendresse, Spanish and Portuguese terneza.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre. Compare Aromanian toartsiri.
From toca (“to chop, mince”) + -ană, from Vulgar Latin *toccare (“to knock, strike”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis.

parole.motivo_incerta: Unknown; Possibly; ipotesi scartata nel testo
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *trufa, or also suggested to be from Ancient Greek τροφή (trophḗ), though this is unlikely. More likely is a feminine derivation ultimately from Latin triumphus, which would make it a doublet of triumf (compare Italian tronfio).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trunclus, from syncopation of Latin trunculus, from truncus.

parole.significato: to crop, shear, clip, trim, prune, mow
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tondĕre, a variant of Latin tondēre, from Proto-Indo-European *tend-, from *temh₂- (“to cut”).
From a Vulgar Latin *tōnsionāre, from Late Latin tōnsiō, tōnsiōnem, from Latin tondeō.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tando, a demonstrative form to Latin quandō (“when”) (whence Romanian când), after the model of Classical Latin quālis ~ tālis, quantus ~ tantus. Compare Neapolitan tanno, Sicilian tànnu, Corsican tandu, Sardinian tando.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tenerus, from Latin tener, tenerum. Compare Aromanian tinir, tiniru, tinãr. Doublet of tandru, which was borrowed from French.
From a Vulgar Latin root *thȳmānea, from Latin thȳmiāma, from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama). Compare Sardinian timanza, timagna, Old French timoine; cf. also Aromanian timnjamã.
Possibly from the variant form trăgăna, from Vulgar Latin *tragīnāre, from *tragere, ultimately from Latin trahō. Compare French traîner, Spanish and Portuguese trajinar.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre (“forget”), a frequentative based on Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus). Compare Aromanian ultari. The second sense of "to look at", used reflexively, may have arisen through its use in an expression "a se uita pe sine", to forget oneself, by ext
From a Vulgar Latin root *ollicella, diminutive of Latin olla.

From older îmbla, from Vulgar Latin *amblāre, syncopated form of Latin ambulāre; compare Aromanian imnu, imnari, Megleno-Romanian amnu, amnare, Istro-Romanian omnu, Old Italian ambiare, Occitan amblar.
From Vulgar Latin *implĕre, from Latin implēre. Compare Catalan omplir, Aromanian umplu, Sardinian umprere.
From Vulgar Latin anglus, from Latin angulus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng-, *ang- (“corner, hirn”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.

parole.significato: to climb, ascend, go up, rise
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *oricāre, derived from Latin orior (“rise, appear”).

parole.significato: to follow (go where someone else goes, not in pursuit)
parole.testo: From urmă, perhaps connected to a Vulgar Latin root *osmāre, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Italian ormare, ormeggiare, also Spanish husmear, husmar, Old French osmer, Venetan usmar. Also compare adulmeca.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *orma or Late Latin osma, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ) . Compare Aromanian urmã, Megleno-Romanian urmă, Istriot urma, Italian orma, also Spanish husma, Venetan usma and Friulian olme.
From a Vulgar Latin root *urdīca, from Latin urtīca. Compare Aromanian urdzãcã. Sense 2 has been popularised by influencer Vlad Obu since the early 2020s.

From a Vulgar Latin root *horrīre, from Latin horrēre (“to be afraid”) (other forms or parts of the verb from horrēscere, horrēscō as with many other 4th conjugation verbs); compare Aromanian urãscu; compare change in meaning also in Albanian urrej (“to hate”), Occitan orrir (“to hate, despise”). Se
From an antecessor shared with mentionable variant urușnic, probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *holoserinicus (“silken”), based on Latin holosēricus.
From a Vulgar Latin root *ustia, from Latin ostia, plural of ostium (“door, entrance”). Compare Aromanian ushã, Italian uscio (Old Italian plural form uscia), Old French huis, Occitan ussa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *virdia (see for cognates), from Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis (“green”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vēra, from Latin vēr (“spring”), from earlier *veror, from Proto-Italic *wezor, from Proto-Indo-European *wósr̥ (“spring”). Cognate with Aromanian vearã; more distantly related to Spanish verano and Portuguese verão.

parole.significato: to watch, to monitor, be on the lookout, keep vigil
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viglāre, from Latin vigilāre.
From verde + -eață or Vulgar Latin *virditia. Compare Italian verdezza, Aromanian virdeatsã.
From Vulgar Latin *vīvitia (cf. Aromanian yeatsã). Synchronically viu + -eață.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *vīvula, from Latin vīvus.

parole.significato: vine - often used as viță de vie (grapevine)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vītia, from Latin vītea, from vītis f.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *volvula, from Latin volvō. Compare Aromanian vãrvurã.

parole.significato: small or narrow valley, dale, or dell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vallicella, diminutive of Late Latin vallicula (“small valley”), diminutive of Latin vallis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ventulāre, from Latin ventilāre. Compare Aromanian vintur, vinturari, Sardinian bentulare, vinturà. Compare the borrowed doublet ventila.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂.

parole.significato: pie filled with cabbage, onions, various other vegetables, or fruit
parole.testo: From varză, or less likely a Vulgar Latin root *virdiāria, from *virdia, from Latin viridia. Compare Aromanian virdzari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vituleus, from Latin vitulus. Compare Aromanian vitulj.
Past participle of vedea, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Aromanian vidzut, Italian veduto, French vu (Old French veü).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exbattere. Compare Aromanian zbat, Italian sbattere, Venetan sbàter, sbàtar, Sicilian sbàttiri, Friulian sbati.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvolāre, from Latin ex- + volāre. Compare Aromanian azboair.

parole.significato: to goggle, ogle, stare at intensely and with wide eyes
parole.testo: From zgău, or less likely a Vulgar Latin *excavīre, from Latin cavum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exventāre, from Latin ventus (“wind”). Compare Aromanian zvintu, zvintari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ambi, from Latin ambae as the plurals of ambo. Replaced by the neologism ambii, ultimately from the same source.

parole.significato: to dress up, to get dressed
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbrācāre, from Latin brāca (“pants, trousers”). Compare also Italian imbracare, Spanish embragar, cf. Latin brācātus.

parole.significato: to eat quickly, gobble up, tongue, swallow, lap
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca (“cheek, mouth”). Compare Aromanian mbuc, mbucari, Italian imboccare, French emboucher, Portuguese and Spanish embocar.

Unknown. Several theories have been proposed. One was a derivation from a Vulgar Latin root *imbubiāre, from bubia, but this was later abandoned. Another possibility is Latin imbuere, through a root *imbuviāre, or Latin bubīre (“swell, inflate”).
Maybe from a Vulgar Latin *ambagella, from Latin ambages.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imbibitāre, derived from Latin bibere (“to drink”). Compare Aromanian mbitari.

parole.significato: to press (down upon), step on, tamp, compress
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *impillāre, from Latin pilāre (“ram down, fix firmly”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *implenīre, from Latin plenus (“full”). Compare Aromanian mplinescu, mpliniri, Romansh emplenir, amplanir, Venetan inpinir, inpienir, Catalan emplenar. Compare also Old French plenir.
From împrejur. Another etymology derives it from a Vulgar Latin *pergȳrāre, from Latin per + gȳrāre, with the addition of the prefix în later within Romanian.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.

parole.significato: to lend (to allow to be used temporarily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imprūmūtāre, from Early Medieval Latin imprōmūtuāre, from Latin prōmūtuārī. Compare Aromanian mprumut.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *impungere, from Latin pungere, or with the în- prefix added later in Romanian. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *pungō, from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).

parole.significato: to make up, reconcile, conciliate, come to agreement
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *impācāre, from in + pācāre (“make peaceful, pacify”); or, more likely, the îm- was added later within Romanian to an older form păca.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inaltum, from Latin in + altus (or perhaps from the phrase in altō). The preposition may have been added by influence of înălța (“raise”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *incircāre, from Latin circāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quetus, from Latin quiētus with the prefix în- added later in Romanian from the variant cet. See also the doublet chit, which came later through French.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētāre, from Latin quiētor, with the prefix în- added in Romanian. Compare also Latin inquiētō.

parole.significato: to conclude, end, wrap up, wind up, close
